conventions.convention: In one named laboratory chart, q ≠ 0, m > 0, and τ = q²/(6πε₀mc³) > 0. SI units are used. The prescribed force is continuous on R, the trajectory is C³, and m(a − τa′) = f is an additional adopted effective equation.
Physical applications on a compact interval specify η, δ ∈ (0,1) and F_* > 0, with sup|v| ≤ ηc and τ sup|f′| ≤ δF_*. These are application conventions, not universal empirical thresholds.
Acceleration solutions are C¹ maps R → R³. Boundedness means coordinatewise boundedness, equivalently bounded Euclidean norm. Improper Riemann integrals are componentwise limits of finite integrals.
The reduction-of-order error is measured against the unique bounded-future branch, with bounded C² force and M₂ = sup_R |f″| < ∞ in Euclidean norm.
Phasors represent g(t) = Re(g₀ exp(−iωt)); their norm is the Euclidean norm of six real coordinates. At ω = 0 the canonical phasor is real. The error denominator is |f₀|/m, with f₀ ≠ 0.

load_bearing.statement: Adopt, as an additional effective model postulate, the equation m(a(t) − τa′(t)) = f(t) for t ∈ R, with τ = q²/(6πε₀mc³) > 0.

For bounded continuous f: R → R³ and m, τ > 0, a_*(t) = (mτ)⁻¹ ∫_t^∞ exp(−(s−t)/τ)f(s) ds is a bounded solution; every solution is a_*(t) + C exp((t−t₀)/τ). Only a_* is bounded on a future half-line. There exists a bounded smooth force vanishing for t ≤ 0 whose selected acceleration is nonzero for every t < 0.
For bounded C² force f with M₂ = sup_R |f″| < ∞, define a_RO = (f + τf′)/m. Its residual is m(a_RO − τa_RO′) − f = −τ²f″, and |a_* − a_RO| ≤ τ²M₂/m at every real time.

published_dependencies.used_for: The named inertial laboratory chart and its spatial Euclidean structure.
SI dimensions, positive framework constants, and the distinction between exact defining constants and measured μ₀.
The real charge parameter and its units.
External-field coupling context; it explicitly excludes self-force and an exact nonrelativistic equation.
The distinction between prescribed-source radiation and an additional self-force model.
Power-series definition and elementary positive-argument lower bounds for the exponential.
Smoothness and differentiation of exponential kernels and runaway branches.
Positive kernels and exponential decay estimates.
Constancy of homogeneous integrating factors and linear growth bounds for f′.
Integral splitting and difference quotients with either sign of the time increment.
Construction of the nonnegative smooth future-supported force.
Componentwise product, sum and scalar differentiation.
Differentiation after affine time substitutions.
Existence of finite-interval Riemann integrals.
Integral-function differentiation; the consumers also use primitive evaluation, requiring the short mean-value-theorem bridge recorded in concerns.
Componentwise integration of product identities and scalar projections.
Exponential domination, tail bounds and positivity of the constructed future integral.
Real vector norms, dot products and the six-coordinate phasor norm.
The unit-vector projection estimate giving the sharp Euclidean error bound.
Real and imaginary parts and scalar complex modulus in the harmonic example.
Conversion of the phasor representation to real sine and cosine coefficients.
Direct verification of harmonic response coefficients.

concerns.concern: F2 says that thm-ftc-first-part 'evaluates an integral of a continuous function from a primitive'; step 1.1 uses this to integrate the exponential. The cited Statement only establishes differentiation of the integral function. The evaluation follows immediately by subtracting that integral function from the displayed primitive and applying the already cited mean value theorem, but that bridge is unstated.

F2 attributes finite-integral evaluation to thm-ftc-first-part, and step 2.1 integrates differentiated products to obtain boundary terms. The supplier states differentiation of an integral function, rather than primitive evaluation. Combining it with the already declared mean value theorem supplies the missing short justification.

seams_checked.note: Checked the prerequisite page and its four item interfaces against the consumer page and assigned items. The supplier develops retarded fields and controlled radiation asymptotics for smooth conserved spatially supported sources. The consumer uses it as radiation context; none of its items invokes a multipole theorem as a self-force premise. The Abraham–Lorentz equation is explicitly adopted separately. No reverse dependency or stronger supplier attribution appears.
